Exam Essentials.title: The Associate lens: use, not build
Exam Essentials.desc: Foundations asks whether you can get reliable work out of Claude as a professional — an analyst, consultant, marketer, compliance officer. It does not ask you to build anything. Items are written from inside a working day: a deadline, a client deliverable, a regulator, a team that has to do this every week.
Exam Essentials.note: When two options are both defensible, pick the one a competent professional could explain to their manager afterwards. Options that require engineering work nobody asked for are usually distractors.

Exam Essentials.title: 60 items, 120 minutes, 720 to pass
Exam Essentials.desc: Scored on a 100–1000 scale with a 720 cut. Two minutes an item — comfortable for recall, tight for a long scenario. Output Evaluation and Validation is the heaviest domain at roughly a fifth of the paper; Troubleshooting and Optimisation is the lightest at about a tenth. Nothing is skippable.
Exam Essentials.note: Weight revision by blueprint share rather than by comfort. This bank also carries a **Technical Awareness** set that is not on the official blueprint — useful for fluency with engineers, filterable if you are optimising purely for the score.

Exam Essentials.title: "MOST appropriate" means read the constraint
Exam Essentials.desc: Several options will describe genuinely good practice. Only one answers the situation the stem actually describes — the stakes, the volume, the audience, the recurrence, the regulation. The exam tests judgement under specifics, not recall of best-practice lists.
Exam Essentials.note: If you can only eliminate an option by saying "that is less good in general", you have the wrong one. A real elimination sounds like "that ignores the fact this runs every week".

Exam Essentials.title: FIRST and NEXT items test sequence
Exam Essentials.desc: Sequencing items hand you several actions that are all eventually correct and ask which comes first. The winner is almost always the diagnostic, reversible, cheap step: find out what is actually wrong, or contain the damage, before changing anything permanent.
Exam Essentials.note: Options that jump straight to the fix — rebuild the rubric, retrain the team, delete the document — are often right in substance and wrong in position. Right answer, wrong turn.

Exam Essentials.title: Multi-select: judge each option alone
Exam Essentials.desc: "Choose TWO" and "Choose THREE" items are scored as a set, but the options do not form a story. Each one is independently true or false against the stem. Picking a plausible partner for the option you are sure about is how people lose these.
Exam Essentials.note: Mark every option true or false on its own before you count. If you end up with four trues, one of them is a general truth the stem never asked about.

Exam Essentials.title: Diagnose before you escalate
Exam Essentials.desc: The reflex answers — a more capable model, a higher plan, a longer prompt, an engineer — are almost never the first move. Most disappointing output traces to missing context, an unstated requirement, or a task that was never a good fit for Claude.
Exam Essentials.note: A stem that says "we upgraded and it did not help" is telling you the problem was never capability. Look for the option that isolates the cause instead of buying a bigger tool.

Exam Essentials.title: Stakes set the standard
Exam Essentials.desc: The same draft can be fine for an internal note and unacceptable in a regulatory filing. Verification depth, review requirements, hedging, disclosure and record-keeping all scale with consequence — who is affected, how reversible it is, and who has to defend it later.
Exam Essentials.note: Scan the stem for the consequence before you scan the options. A patient, a loan applicant, a regulator or a tribunal in the scenario changes which answer is correct.

Exam Essentials.title: Accountability does not transfer
Exam Essentials.desc: Claude produces drafts; a named person owns the result. No configuration, disclosure or audit trail moves responsibility onto the tool, and "the model said so" is never a defence for a decision that harmed someone.
Exam Essentials.note: Any option in which the model, the vendor or the workflow owns an outcome is wrong. The right answer names a human who is accountable and says what they actually did.

Exam Essentials.title: Absolutes are distractor tells
Exam Essentials.desc: Options promising a guarantee — eliminates the need for review, ensures accuracy, always produces, never fabricates, makes verification unnecessary — describe something a probabilistic system cannot do. The same applies to blanket prohibitions no working professional could actually follow.
Exam Essentials.note: Scan for "eliminates", "guarantees", "ensures", "never" and "all". They are not automatically wrong, but they are wrong far more often than they are right, and they are the fastest eliminations available to you.

Exam Essentials.title: Sophistication is not the answer key
Exam Essentials.desc: The most elaborate option — an extra tool, a second model pass, a new Project, a custom build — is a distractor more often than a key. Added machinery has to answer a requirement the stem actually states.
Exam Essentials.note: Ask which sentence in the stem the extra complexity satisfies. If you cannot point at one, take the simpler option that meets the stated need.

Output Evaluation and Validation.title: Fluency is not accuracy
Output Evaluation and Validation.desc: Claude writes clean, confident, well-organised prose whether or not the content is right. Style and correctness are independent axes, so how good an output reads tells you nothing about whether it is true. That is the whole reason verification is a separate step rather than an impression.
Output Evaluation and Validation.note: The stem phrase to watch for is "it read well, so the analyst approved it". Fluency doing the work of evidence is the trap this entire domain is built around.

Output Evaluation and Validation.title: Grounded versus parametric claims
Output Evaluation and Validation.desc: A grounded claim can be traced to material you actually supplied — an uploaded document, a pasted extract, a connected record. A parametric claim comes from what the model absorbed in training. Grounding is about traceability, not truth: a grounded claim can still be wrong, and an ungrounded one can happen to be right.
Output Evaluation and Validation.note: Sort an output into grounded and parametric before you verify anything. Parametric claims about named entities, figures and regulations are where your checking time belongs.

Output Evaluation and Validation.title: Fabrication versus staleness
Output Evaluation and Validation.desc: A fabricated detail never existed — an invented citation, quotation, statistic, case reference or product feature. A stale one was true and no longer is, because training has a horizon. Both arrive as a confident wrong sentence, and they need different remedies.
Output Evaluation and Validation.note: If the claim is the kind of thing that changes — prices, rates, org charts, regulations — suspect staleness and supply a current source. If it is oddly specific and hard to locate, suspect fabrication.

Output Evaluation and Validation.title: Triage what you verify
Output Evaluation and Validation.desc: You cannot check every sentence, so rank by consequence and checkability. Named sources, figures, dates, quotations, legal and regulatory references, and anything a reader will act on come first. Generic framing and restated input come last.
Output Evaluation and Validation.note: Checking the easy claims and skipping the load-bearing one is verification theatre. A review that felt thorough but missed the number in the recommendation is exactly this failure.

Output Evaluation and Validation.title: Check against the source, not against Claude
Output Evaluation and Validation.desc: Verification means comparing the output to the document, the system of record, or the original data. Asking Claude whether its own answer is correct tests internal consistency, not grounding — the same process that produced the claim is being asked to confirm it.
Output Evaluation and Validation.note: Self-critique is genuinely useful for format, completeness and contradiction. When the stem asks how to confirm a figure or a citation, the answer always leaves the conversation.

Output Evaluation and Validation.title: Omission is the error you will not see
Output Evaluation and Validation.desc: Commission errors — something wrong on the page — get caught because they are visible. Omission errors are the clause the summary dropped, the outlier a multi-document synthesis smoothed over, the exception a policy digest lost. Reading the output cannot reveal them.
Output Evaluation and Validation.note: Completeness is checked against the source or the brief, never against the output. Any option proposing to review the summary on its own is not checking for omissions.

Output Evaluation and Validation.title: Recompute, do not re-read
Output Evaluation and Validation.desc: Numbers are where confident output fails quietly. Totals that do not sum, unit conversions, percentage points confused with percent, relative versus absolute change, and compounding applied once too often all survive a careful read, because every individual line looks reasonable.
Output Evaluation and Validation.note: An arithmetic error early in a chain propagates into every figure after it. When a stem reports one wrong number, check whether the rest were derived from it.

Output Evaluation and Validation.title: Self-consistency in a long output
Output Evaluation and Validation.desc: Long documents contradict themselves. The executive summary states a figure the appendix disproves; a term is defined one way in section two and another in section five; the recommendation does not follow from the risk register printed beneath it.
Output Evaluation and Validation.note: Cross-section contradiction is the failure reviewers miss, because they read sequentially. Compare the summary against the body deliberately — it is the part people actually act on.

Output Evaluation and Validation.title: Sycophancy under pushback
Output Evaluation and Validation.desc: Push back on a correct answer and Claude may abandon it, agreeing with confidence and reasoning backwards to your position. Seniority, certainty and simple repetition all trigger it. The reversal arrives with no new evidence, and that is the tell.
Output Evaluation and Validation.note: Probe neutrally — "what is the basis for that figure?" — rather than asserting the opposite. Agreement that appears the moment you object is not a second opinion.

Output Evaluation and Validation.title: Acceptance criteria before you read
Output Evaluation and Validation.desc: Decide what good enough means before the output exists: which dimensions matter — accuracy, completeness against the brief, tone and brand fit, absence of biased framing — the threshold for each, and what stakes justify that threshold. A rubric names the criteria; a golden set shows what passing looks like.
Output Evaluation and Validation.note: Criteria written after seeing the output are shaped by it. Rubrics and golden sets also go stale: when the standard moves and the reference examples do not, good work starts failing review.

Workflow Integration and Solution Design.title: Volume and repeatability are fit signals
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.desc: A task is worth building a workflow around when it recurs, follows a stable shape, and produces output someone can actually check. Volume on its own justifies nothing — a thousand instances of a task with unclear criteria just produces a thousand problems faster.
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.note: Stems lead with an impressive number of cases per month. Confirm the other two signals before accepting it as a fit; volume is necessary, not sufficient.

Workflow Integration and Solution Design.title: Some tasks should not be automated
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.desc: Poor fit is not about difficulty. It is tasks whose criteria cannot be articulated, tasks whose value is the relationship, decisions with serious consequences for a named person, and — most dangerous — tasks where a wrong answer is invisible to whoever reviews it.
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.note: The worst combination is high volume plus invisible errors. If nobody can tell a good output from a bad one at review speed, more throughput is just more undetected error.

Workflow Integration and Solution Design.title: Decompose the process, not the job
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.desc: Map the end-to-end process step by step, then mark each step Claude-assisted, human, or human-with-Claude. Most real processes split cleanly: drafting, extraction, comparison and summarising move; judgement calls, negotiation, and sign-off stay where they were.
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.note: The right answer is usually a decomposition rather than a verdict on the whole process. Options that automate everything or nothing are both dodging the question.

Workflow Integration and Solution Design.title: Batch versus interactive
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.desc: If nobody is waiting for the answer, work can be queued, run in bulk and reviewed later, which changes both the economics and how you design review. Batch needs inputs stable enough that one set of instructions works across the whole run.
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.note: "Reviewed the next morning" signals batch. But batch multiplies a systematic error across every item, so it needs deliberate sampling at the end that interactive work gets for free.

Workflow Integration and Solution Design.title: Checkpoint, gate, straight-through
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.desc: A review checkpoint informs someone; an approval gate blocks progress until a person signs; straight-through processing has neither. Reversibility decides which you need — anything that pays, sends, commits or decides about a person needs a gate in front of it.
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.note: Straight-through processing should be a visible decision in the design, not a default that arrives because nobody specified a gate. Ask what the process does if the output is wrong.

Workflow Integration and Solution Design.title: Escalation and fallback are different
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.desc: Fallback answers what happens when Claude is unavailable, fails, or refuses — the work still has to get done that day. Escalation answers what happens when the output is fine but the case is beyond the workflow's remit: unusual, ambiguous, or above a risk threshold.
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.note: A real escalation path has named owners, trigger conditions, and somewhere for the case to go when the first owner is at capacity. "Send it to a human" is not a path.

Workflow Integration and Solution Design.title: Handoff to the system of record
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.desc: Value is realised where the output lands — the CRM, the claims system, the case file. Specify the handoff: which fields, in what shape, after which approval, and what happens if the transfer half-completes. A connector that can write needs tighter scope than one that only reads.
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.note: Watch for write-back scope creep in a stem: a connector added for one report quietly acquiring the ability to change records nobody reviews.

Workflow Integration and Solution Design.title: Design for auditability up front
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.desc: Someone will ask, months later, why this output was produced and why it was accepted. Answering needs the input, the instruction or prompt version in force at the time, the output, and who reviewed it when. None of it is reconstructable afterwards if it was never captured.
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.note: Options that propose rebuilding an audit trail from chat history after an incident are describing the failure, not the fix. Auditability is designed in before launch.

Workflow Integration and Solution Design.title: Pilot against a measured baseline
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.desc: A pilot proves something only if you knew the starting point and agreed in advance what result justifies rolling out. Measure the current time, cost and error rate first, set the threshold, then run on a representative slice rather than the easiest cases.
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.note: A pilot with no pre-agreed success criteria always succeeds, which is why it is worthless as evidence. Choose a use case that is real but recoverable if it fails.

Workflow Integration and Solution Design.title: Templates, runbooks and sunsetting
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.desc: One person's good prompt becomes a team capability only when it is written down — a shared template, a documented workflow someone else can run, and an owner who keeps both current. Uneven adoption is usually an enablement gap rather than resistance.
Workflow Integration and Solution Design.note: Workflows also end. When the process has changed, usage has drifted, or the value never appeared, retiring it deliberately beats letting it rot into a source of stale output.

Prompting and Task Execution.title: The five building blocks
Prompting and Task Execution.desc: Role, context, task, constraints, format. Role sets the frame; context supplies what Claude cannot know; task states the job; constraints bound it; format shapes the output. Most disappointing results are one missing block rather than a limit of the model.
Prompting and Task Execution.note: Every prompt contains all five whether you write them or not — anything left out gets filled with a default. These five words are the vocabulary the rest of the domain uses.

Prompting and Task Execution.title: Specificity: say what good looks like
Prompting and Task Execution.desc: "Professional", "concise" and "engaging" are labels, not specifications; every reader fills them differently and so does Claude. Replace them with something checkable — who the reader is, how long, what must appear, what a successful version would let that reader do.
Prompting and Task Execution.note: Stating the success criteria inside the prompt is the cheapest quality lever available. If you cannot tell from the prompt whether an output passed, neither can Claude.

Prompting and Task Execution.title: Context versus reference material
Prompting and Task Execution.desc: Context is the situation only you know — the history of the account, why the last version was rejected, which stakeholder must not be surprised. Reference material is source text you supply so the answer comes from a document instead of from recall.
Prompting and Task Execution.note: Two different symptoms. Output that misreads the situation needs context; output full of plausible but unverifiable facts needs reference material. A stem showing both wants both.

Prompting and Task Execution.title: Role prompting is a frame, not authority
Prompting and Task Execution.desc: Asking Claude to act as an actuary or a solicitor changes vocabulary, structure, and which considerations surface first. It does not make the output professionally authoritative, compliant, or safe to send unreviewed, and it does not add knowledge the model did not have.
Prompting and Task Execution.note: Any option where a persona makes advice qualified, or removes the need for a professional to check it, is wrong. Persona changes register, never accountability.

Prompting and Task Execution.title: Tell Claude to ask instead of guess
Prompting and Task Execution.desc: Given an ambiguous brief, Claude will pick an interpretation and produce a confident answer on it. An explicit instruction to raise clarifying questions before starting converts a silent wrong assumption into a cheap question asked at the right moment.
Prompting and Task Execution.note: Most useful where the ambiguity is about intent rather than a missing input you could simply have supplied. Place it plainly: "if the scope is unclear, ask before drafting".

Prompting and Task Execution.title: Few-shot: show, do not describe
Prompting and Task Execution.desc: Examples carry conventions prose cannot state — house style, how an edge case is handled, how much detail a field takes. Representativeness matters far more than count: a few examples spanning the real variety beat many that all look alike.
Prompting and Task Execution.note: Examples sharing an accidental pattern teach that pattern. If every example is a clean case, expect the messy ones to be forced into the same shape.

Prompting and Task Execution.title: Step-by-step reasoning: when it pays
Prompting and Task Execution.desc: Asking Claude to work through a problem in stages helps where the answer depends on several interacting constraints or a calculation — comparing clauses, applying eligibility rules, reconciling figures. On drafting, summarising and formatting it mostly adds length.
Prompting and Task Execution.note: Visible reasoning is not verified reasoning. A tidy chain of steps can still reach a wrong conclusion, and the exam likes options that treat shown workings as proof.

Prompting and Task Execution.title: Delimiters and where the document goes
Prompting and Task Execution.desc: When a prompt mixes instructions with content, mark the boundary — XML-style tags or clearly labelled sections — so Claude does not read the document as instructions or your instructions as text to summarise. With long material, put the document first and the question after it.
Prompting and Task Execution.note: Missing delimiters is the usual cause of Claude answering about your prompt rather than your document, or obeying a sentence that was sitting inside the source text.

Prompting and Task Execution.title: One prompt, one job
Prompting and Task Execution.desc: A prompt asking for a summary, a risk assessment, a client email and a slide outline will do all four adequately and none well. Split the work into stages, feeding each one what the previous stage produced rather than bundling everything into a single request.
Prompting and Task Execution.note: Two anti-patterns share this root: the kitchen-sink prompt, and the buried ask where the real request sits mid-paragraph and gets treated as background colour.

Prompting and Task Execution.title: Positive framing and explicit format
Prompting and Task Execution.desc: Tell Claude what to do rather than what to avoid; a list of prohibitions still puts the forbidden material in front of it and leaves the target undefined. Then specify the shape concretely — headings, a table with named columns, a word or item count.
Prompting and Task Execution.note: Where a stem shows repeated near-misses on length or depth, one example of an acceptable output fixes it faster than another adjective ever will.

Technical Awareness.title: Tokens are the unit of cost
Technical Awareness.desc: Models read and write in tokens — fragments of words rather than characters. Everything you send counts: instructions, the pasted document, attached knowledge, and the conversation so far, not just the reply. For document-heavy work the input side usually dominates the bill.
Technical Awareness.note: A stem reporting high cost alongside short answers is pointing at input. The lever is sending less — trimming context — not shortening the response.

Technical Awareness.title: Context window versus output length
Technical Awareness.desc: The context window is how much the model can hold at once: prompt, documents and conversation together. 200K tokens is the figure usually quoted for Claude. Maximum output length is a separate and much smaller ceiling on a single reply. They are independent limits that fail differently.
Technical Awareness.note: Output stopping mid-sentence is the reply ceiling and needs continuation. Earlier material being ignored is context pressure and needs less input or a fresh start.

Technical Awareness.title: Signals a workflow outgrew chat
Technical Awareness.desc: Chat stops being the right surface when the same task runs on a schedule, when volume exceeds what a person will paste, when results must flow into another system automatically, or when the capability has to sit inside something customers use.
Technical Awareness.note: "Someone does this forty times every morning" is an API signal. "Someone does this well, occasionally" is not — the API buys automation, not better answers.

Technical Awareness.title: The API-level dials
Technical Awareness.desc: Past the chat interface you get a system prompt holding standing instructions for every call, a temperature setting trading consistency against variety, and the ability to name a specific model version rather than tracking the newest one.
Technical Awareness.note: Low temperature makes output more consistent, not deterministic. A system prompt is an instruction, not a security boundary and not a secret. Pinning a version means upgrades become a decision you test, rather than a change that arrives unannounced.

Technical Awareness.title: Rate limits are a capacity constraint
Technical Awareness.desc: Providers cap how much you can send in a period. Hitting a limit produces errors and delays, not worse answers, and it usually bites when a batch fires all at once rather than when total daily volume is high.
Technical Awareness.note: Failures that cluster at a peak and clear afterwards are rate limiting. The fix is queuing, spreading and retrying with a delay — never a different model.

Technical Awareness.title: Retrieval versus a long context
Technical Awareness.desc: You can put documents straight into the prompt, or use retrieval to search a large collection and insert only the passages that match. Long context is simpler and complete; retrieval scales to material that could never fit, at the cost of sometimes fetching the wrong passage.
Technical Awareness.note: Retrieval failures look like confident answers built on the wrong extract. When a stem says the answer was well-grounded but about the wrong policy, suspect retrieval rather than the model.

Technical Awareness.title: Tool use, function calling and MCP
Technical Awareness.desc: Tool use lets a model request an action — look up a record, run a search, file a ticket — and use what comes back. MCP is a standard way of exposing those systems so each integration is not bespoke. Whatever returns becomes context the model then relies on.
Technical Awareness.note: The failure modes are choosing the wrong tool, passing bad arguments, and treating a tool result as an instruction. Anything that writes, sends or spends needs a check outside the model.

Technical Awareness.title: Agents versus a single call
Technical Awareness.desc: A single call does one defined thing. An agent chooses its own next steps, calling tools in a sequence nobody wrote in advance. That suits genuinely open-ended work and costs predictability — each step can be slightly wrong, and the errors compound down the chain.
Technical Awareness.note: Agents earn their place when the steps cannot be listed beforehand. If you can write the sequence down, a fixed sequence is cheaper, testable, and far easier to explain to an auditor.

Technical Awareness.title: Caching and batch: the structural levers
Technical Awareness.desc: Prompt caching reuses a large stable opening — the same manual or instruction set across many calls — instead of reprocessing it every time. Batch processing trades immediacy for cheaper throughput on work nobody is waiting for.
Technical Awareness.note: Caching only helps when the front of the prompt is genuinely unchanged; a timestamp or user name at the top defeats it. Batch only helps when no one needs the answer now.

Technical Awareness.title: API keys are credentials
Technical Awareness.desc: A key authenticates whatever holds it and has no idea who is using it. Pasted into a shared document, a prompt, a spreadsheet or a public repository, it becomes a credential anyone can spend against. SSO governs people; keys govern programs, and the two are not interchangeable.
Technical Awareness.note: On exposure, revoke and reissue first and investigate second. Separate keys per environment and per team are what make that possible without taking everything else down.

Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.title: Classify the data before you paste
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.desc: Personal data, health information, cardholder data, client-confidential material and commercially sensitive plans each carry different obligations, and one document often contains several at once. Classification is the step that determines everything after it — which account, which controls, whether the task proceeds at all.
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.note: Combinations matter more than individual fields. A postcode, a job title and a date of birth identify a person even though none of them is a name.

Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.title: Minimise before you protect
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.desc: The strongest control is not sending the data at all. Strip or mask what the task does not need, work from extracts rather than whole files, and re-attach identifiers afterwards if the output requires them. Redaction that leaves the person identifiable from the surrounding context has not worked.
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.note: Prefer the option that reduces what leaves your boundary over the one that wraps a control around sending everything. Over-redaction that makes the task impossible is also a wrong answer.

Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.title: Consumer versus enterprise posture
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.desc: Which account the work runs on determines the data-handling terms in force — retention, whether inputs may be used for improvement, where processing happens, and whether the vendor will sign the agreements a regulated client requires. These are contractual and configuration matters, not things to infer.
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.note: Regulated or client-confidential work on a personal account is a governance finding however careful the individual was. Check the surface before you check the prompt.

Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.title: Decision support, not decision authority
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.desc: Hiring, lending, clinical, disciplinary, benefits, legal and safety decisions need a human who exercises judgement and owns the outcome. Claude may summarise, surface considerations or draft the rationale; it may not be the thing that decides. A reviewer who approves everything at speed is not oversight.
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.note: Real oversight means time to disagree, access to the underlying evidence, a record of overrides, and consequences that land on the human. Volume that makes disagreement impossible is the tell.

Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.title: Disclosure, consent and notice
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.desc: Disclosure tells the affected person AI was involved. Notice tells them their data is being processed and how. Consent asks permission and can be withdrawn. They are three separate obligations, and satisfying one does not satisfy another.
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.note: Disclosure is not explanation — saying AI was used does not tell someone why they were declined. Consent buried in terms nobody reads is a common wrong answer dressed as compliance.

Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.title: The professional-advice boundary
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.desc: General information about how a rule, condition or product works is different from advice applied to one person's circumstances. The second is what is regulated in law, medicine and finance, and it is what a Claude output must not become without a qualified professional standing behind it.
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.note: Watch for a scenario drifting from explaining a policy to telling a named individual what to do. Safety-critical topics also need a real referral path, not a softer disclaimer.

Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.title: Bias in consequential decisions
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.desc: Bias enters through the historical data a process was built on, through proxy variables that stand in for protected characteristics, and through the framing of the prompt itself. Deleting the obvious field does not remove the effect, because the remaining fields still carry it.
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.note: Fairness is demonstrated by testing outcomes across groups, not by intent. An option that fixes bias by instructing Claude to be unbiased is always wrong.

Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.title: Prompt injection from untrusted content
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.desc: Instructions can hide inside anything you feed in — a supplier's PDF, a forwarded email, a web page, a record returned by a connector. Claude cannot reliably tell content from commands, so treat everything arriving from outside as data rather than direction.
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.note: The risk becomes real the moment a workflow both reads untrusted material and can act on it. Keep consequential steps behind a person or a check that lives outside the conversation.

Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.title: Shadow AI is a symptom
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.desc: Unsanctioned use happens because the approved route is slow, missing or unusable and the work still has to get done. Banning it moves the activity out of sight. The durable response is a sanctioned path easier than the workaround, plus a way to admit past use without punishment.
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.note: The right answer usually pairs a control with an enablement step. Detection and policy alone are marked down, because neither addresses why people went around you.

Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.title: When AI output causes harm
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.desc: An AI incident rarely looks like an outage — the system worked and the output was wrong, or went somewhere it should not have. The order is the same as any incident: contain, establish scope, notify whoever must be told, then fix the cause and record what happened.
Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use.note: Scope means every downstream use, not just the original output. A wrong figure that reached a filing, a client and a dashboard is three remediations, not one.

Product and Model Selection.title: The tiers are a trade, not a ladder
Product and Model Selection.desc: Haiku, Sonnet and Opus differ in speed, cost and reasoning depth. They are not good, better and best for every task — the fast tier is the correct answer for narrow high-volume work, where the deepest tier simply burns money and time. Sonnet is the sensible default.
Product and Model Selection.note: Start from the balanced tier and justify any move off it with something in the stem: a latency target, a volume, or reasoning the default demonstrably could not do.

Product and Model Selection.title: Domain complexity is not cognitive complexity
Product and Model Selection.desc: A task can be about a difficult subject and still be simple work — pulling defined fields from a clinical report, tagging legal correspondence by matter type. What justifies the deepest tier is novel reasoning across domains with no established pattern to follow.
Product and Model Selection.note: "This is important and technical" is not an argument for the top tier. Ask whether the task is really pattern matching wearing specialist clothing.

Product and Model Selection.title: Mixed-tier pipelines: choose per step
Product and Model Selection.desc: Tier is a per-step decision, not a per-system one. A pipeline can filter and classify on the fast tier, spend on the step where judgement actually determines the outcome, then format the result cheaply again. Most of the volume in a workflow is not the part needing depth.
Product and Model Selection.note: Downgrading a step is safe when it is tightly specified and its output is checked downstream. Downgrading the step that carries the judgement is where quality quietly disappears.

Product and Model Selection.title: Escalation often masks a prompt problem
Product and Model Selection.desc: Output that is generic, off-format or answering the wrong question rarely improves on a more capable tier, because the cause was missing context or an unstated requirement. Moving up the tiers conceals that for a while and multiplies what it costs.
Product and Model Selection.note: The diagnostic is whether the same prompt with better context and clearer criteria improves the result. If it does, this was never a tier problem.

Product and Model Selection.title: Extended thinking: when it pays
Product and Model Selection.desc: Extra reasoning before answering helps where the conclusion depends on weighing several interacting factors — a negotiation position, a multi-clause contract, a strategy trade-off. On drafting, formatting and summarising it adds cost and waiting without changing the answer.
Product and Model Selection.note: It is a different lever from tier. Output that is competent but shallow points here; a model that cannot perform the task at all points at tier.

Product and Model Selection.title: Context-window pressure as a factor
Product and Model Selection.desc: When the material is very long, the binding constraint stops being reasoning depth and becomes how much can be attended to at once. Coverage degrades before anything visibly breaks: detail in the middle of a long input carries less weight than material at either end.
Product and Model Selection.note: The fix is usually several passes over sections, or ordering the input so what matters is not buried in the middle — not a more capable model.

Product and Model Selection.title: Match the surface to the work
Product and Model Selection.desc: Web, desktop and mobile suit interactive individual work at different intensities; Claude Code is built for engineers working in a codebase; the API is for embedding and automation. Choose the least elaborate surface that does the job.
Product and Model Selection.note: A stem describing non-technical users with an occasional task, answered with Claude Code or an API build, is the classic over-engineering distractor.

Product and Model Selection.title: Artifacts versus inline output
Product and Model Selection.desc: Artifacts put substantial self-contained output — a document, a table, a piece of code, a rendered page — into its own panel you can iterate on, copy and share without dragging the conversation along. Short answers and discussion belong inline.
Product and Model Selection.note: The signal is whether the output is a deliverable that will be revised or handed on. Asking a question about a document does not need one.

Product and Model Selection.title: Research mode is not a search box
Product and Model Selection.desc: Research mode runs an extended multi-source investigation of the public web and reports back with sources. It is slower and heavier than an ordinary answer, it cannot see inside your organisation, and its sources still need reading rather than trusting.
Product and Model Selection.note: It answers "what is out there about this", not "what does our policy say". A citation is evidence that a page exists, not that it supports the sentence attached to it.

Product and Model Selection.title: A plan upgrade is not a quality fix
Product and Model Selection.desc: Plan tiers govern access and how much you can use, not how well Claude reasons. Output that is vague, off-brief or wrongly formatted stays that way on a higher plan, and hitting a usage limit is a capacity signal rather than a quality one.
Product and Model Selection.note: When a stem pairs disappointing output with a suggestion to upgrade the subscription, the answer lies in the prompt, the context, or the choice of task.

Troubleshooting and Optimisation.title: Map the symptom to the missing element
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.desc: Each recurring failure points at one part of the prompt. Generic output means missing context; the wrong shape means no format specification; the wrong register means the audience was never named; an answer to a different question means the task statement was ambiguous.
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.note: Name the symptom precisely before choosing a fix. Options that respond to a different symptom than the stem describes are the most common distractor in this domain.

Troubleshooting and Optimisation.title: Change one variable at a time
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.desc: When three things change at once and the output improves, you have learned nothing reusable. Adjust one element, rerun, compare. Testing in a fresh chat removes the accumulated conversation that would otherwise be an equally good explanation for the difference.
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.note: A stem where someone rewrote the prompt, switched tier and attached a document, then asks what fixed it, is testing this. The honest answer is that it cannot be known.

Troubleshooting and Optimisation.title: Inconsistent runs are normal
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.desc: The same prompt will not produce identical output twice. Variation that stays inside the brief is expected behaviour. Variation that crosses it — sometimes six sections, sometimes three — means the brief left room, not that anything is broken.
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.note: Tighten the specification and add an example rather than rerunning until you get a good one. Rerolling is not a fix, and it does not survive being handed to a colleague.

Troubleshooting and Optimisation.title: Refusals on legitimate work
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.desc: Professional tasks can trip caution — security write-ups, clinical language, fraud investigations, adversarial scenarios. The usual cause is a request that looks like something else because no purpose, role or setting was stated. Supplying that professional context resolves most of them.
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.note: Distinguish refusal from truncation: a refusal explains itself, a truncation stops mid-thought. Persistent refusal on a genuinely restricted topic is a boundary, not a prompt bug.

Troubleshooting and Optimisation.title: More context is not better
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.desc: Attaching documents and background the task does not need dilutes the material that matters and gives Claude irrelevant things to weigh. Past the point of sufficiency, extra context makes output vaguer rather than richer, and it pushes the material you actually care about further from the question.
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.note: When quality dropped after someone added more material, suspect noise. The fix is removing, which is the opposite of the instinct the rest of the syllabus trains.

Troubleshooting and Optimisation.title: Truncation and continuation
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.desc: Output stopping mid-sentence or mid-table has hit the reply ceiling; it is not a refusal. Recovering cleanly means naming exactly where to resume — the last complete section or row — rather than saying "continue", which invites a restart or a silent gap.
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.note: If it truncates every time, the request is too large for one reply. Split it by section rather than continuing repeatedly and stitching the seams together.

Troubleshooting and Optimisation.title: Drift and the fresh-chat decision
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.desc: Long threads accumulate superseded instructions, abandoned directions and earlier drafts, all of which still influence the answer. Output slowly stops matching the current request. Restating the instruction sometimes recovers it; past a point only a clean start does.
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.note: Before restarting, copy out the working prompt and the best output so far. The cost of a fresh chat is the context you lose, so capture it deliberately rather than rebuilding from memory.

Troubleshooting and Optimisation.title: Content in the middle gets missed
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.desc: In a long document, material at the beginning and the end carries more weight than material in the middle. A clause buried deep can be read and still not surface in the summary, which looks like a comprehension failure but is a position effect.
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.note: Point at it: name the section, ask for a pass structured section by section, or split the file. A stem where one specific mid-document term was omitted is this, not fabrication.

Troubleshooting and Optimisation.title: Cost and latency are separate problems
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.desc: Waiting is driven mostly by how much gets generated; spending is driven mostly by how much gets sent, especially with large attachments and long conversations. The two do not answer to the same lever, and a stem naming a deadline is not naming a budget.
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.note: Optimising past the quality floor is its own failure. Cutting context to save money and quietly losing accuracy nobody measures is a wrong answer even when the arithmetic works.

Troubleshooting and Optimisation.title: When it is not a prompt problem
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.desc: Iteration has a stopping point. Persistent failure on the same task after context, specification and examples have all been tried usually means the task is a poor fit, the source material is inadequate, or something is broken outside the conversation entirely.
Troubleshooting and Optimisation.note: Errors, outages and access failures go to IT with what you tried and when. A task needing judgement, accountability, or knowledge nobody supplied will not be fixed by a better prompt.

Configuration and Knowledge Management.title: The recurrence test for a Project
Configuration and Knowledge Management.desc: A Project earns its keep when the same context is re-supplied every time — the same role, the same standards, the same reference documents. Instructions and knowledge persist across sessions in a way a conversation does not. A task done once, however important, does not need one.
Configuration and Knowledge Management.note: Look for a stem that quantifies repeated setup: minutes lost per session, every week. That, not the seniority of the user or the sensitivity of the work, is what justifies a Project.

Configuration and Knowledge Management.title: Instructions versus knowledge
Configuration and Knowledge Management.desc: Custom instructions say how to behave — role, standards, tone, format, what never to do. Project knowledge is the reference material facts should come from. A policy document pasted into instructions bloats them; a formatting rule hidden inside a document gets buried.
Configuration and Knowledge Management.note: The test is whether the content is a behaviour or a source. Instructions reciting facts, and knowledge bases carrying style guidance, are both misfiled and both produce the same drift.

Configuration and Knowledge Management.title: Actionable, not aspirational
Configuration and Knowledge Management.desc: "Write with warmth and authority" produces different output for every person on a team, because it describes an impression rather than a behaviour. Instructions have to be checkable: the register, the length, the structure, the terms to use and the terms to avoid.
Configuration and Knowledge Management.note: The diagnostic for a vague instruction is variation across users following the same Project. If two colleagues get materially different shapes of output, the instruction described a feeling.

Configuration and Knowledge Management.title: Precedence and partial override
Configuration and Knowledge Management.desc: A per-chat prompt overrides the project instruction on the dimension it addresses and leaves the rest in force. Asking for bullet points changes the format; it does not switch off the tone, the audience, or the standing prohibitions you configured.
Configuration and Knowledge Management.note: Write safety-critical rules as explicit prohibitions rather than preferences. A stated "never" holds up against a casual per-chat request far better than an implied norm does.

Configuration and Knowledge Management.title: Instruction bloat degrades compliance
Configuration and Knowledge Management.desc: An instruction set that grows every time someone is disappointed ends up long, internally contradictory, and followed less reliably than a short one. Every addition competes with the rest for attention, and rules written for problems that no longer exist stay in forever.
Configuration and Knowledge Management.note: The remedy is pruning to the instructions that demonstrably change the output, not adding one more clarifying line. Schedule a review rather than waiting for a visible failure.

Configuration and Knowledge Management.title: A shared Project is a control
Configuration and Knowledge Management.desc: Sharing a Project is how a team produces work that looks like it came from one place, and how a new joiner starts at the standard rather than learning it by osmosis. It also concentrates risk: everyone with access sees every document inside it.
Configuration and Knowledge Management.note: Decide separately who may read and who may edit, and keep client- or matter-specific material out of any Project shared beyond that engagement. Confidentiality failures here are structural, not accidental.

Configuration and Knowledge Management.title: Curate, do not accumulate
Configuration and Knowledge Management.desc: A knowledge base is not a filing cabinet. Every document that is not needed for the task competes with the ones that are, so relevance falls as the collection grows. Scope creep — another workstream's material drifting in — shows up as answers drawn from the wrong context.
Configuration and Knowledge Management.note: Signals it needs curation: output citing material from a different workstream, steady growth with no removals, and nobody able to say what is actually in there.

Configuration and Knowledge Management.title: Superseded and conflicting documents
Configuration and Knowledge Management.desc: Two versions of the same template, or a retired policy sitting beside its replacement, give Claude no way to know which one governs. Answers become inconsistent between sessions for no visible reason, and the older document does not reliably lose.
Configuration and Knowledge Management.note: Remove the superseded version rather than adding a note saying which is current. If it genuinely cannot be deleted yet, state in the instructions which document governs.

Configuration and Knowledge Management.title: Structure documents for retrieval
Configuration and Knowledge Management.desc: Names and headings are what make a document findable and its sections distinguishable. "Policy_v3_final" tells nobody what it covers, and a wall of unstructured text offers no anchor. Split a file when it covers genuinely separate subjects; keep it whole when the sections are read together.
Configuration and Knowledge Management.note: Splitting is for distinct subjects, not for size alone. Breaking one coherent procedure into fragments destroys the connections that made it answerable in the first place.

Configuration and Knowledge Management.title: Connector, upload, or per-chat file
Configuration and Knowledge Management.desc: A connector reads live from the source, so it suits data changing faster than anyone will re-upload. Project knowledge suits stable reference material. A per-chat upload suits one-off documents and sensitive material that should not persist for everyone with access.
Configuration and Knowledge Management.note: The deciding questions are how fast the content changes and who should keep seeing it. A daily report loaded as static knowledge is stale the day after it goes in.
